narrative: The model estimated a 61.2% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above 50%, the application was denied: the school treated first-time bar failure as more likely than success. The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in decile 1, well below the accepted-student average of 5.79, and this factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor and, in this assessment, it worked slightly in your favor, reducing the predicted risk; even so, a score of 35 is below the accepted-student average of 37.18, so it should not be treated as a reliable strength. Your first-year class standing was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure: decile 2 versus an accepted-student average of 6.00. Thus the denial was driven mainly by persistently low class standing across law school, with only a modest countervailing signal from the LSAT. Next, ask admissions for feedback, focus on raising upper-level grades or class standing, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve it. You may also strengthen your application with bar-readiness coursework, study support, and a clear academic-improvement plan before reapplying or applying elsewhere.
